stem: A healthy volunteer jogs on a treadmill inside a chamber while the inspired PO2 is lowered from 160 mm Hg to 60 mm Hg.
oneliner: Healthy volunteer jogging + inspired PO2 160 → 60 mm Hg → which pressure rises?
ask: The fall in inspired PO2 is most likely to increase which of the following?

whyNot.A: Low PO2 relaxes **systemic** arterioles, so it gives no reason for diastolic pressure to rise; its specific effect is in the **lung**
whyNot.C: The only change made is **inspired PO2**, which acts on the pulmonary bed, not on systemic pulse pressure
whyNot.D: Low PO2 **dilates** systemic vessels, so mean systemic pressure is not the pressure it raises
whyNot.E: Lowering **inspired PO2** acts on lung arterioles; it gives no specific push to systemic systolic pressure

why: Low alveolar PO2 makes **pulmonary arterioles constrict** (hypoxic pulmonary vasoconstriction), the opposite of the systemic response. With the whole lung hypoxic, **resistance and mean pulmonary artery pressure rise** across the board.

idea.rule: Hypoxia constricts pulmonary vessels and dilates systemic ones.
also: High altitude pulmonary hypertension
Chronic COPD with cor pulmonale
Local airway obstruction (blood diverted to ventilated alveoli)
Sleep apnea with nocturnal hypoxia

stem: A 58-year-old woman has had two years of progressive breathlessness on exertion and a dry cough. She has fine crackles at both lung bases and clubbed fingers. Spirometry shows reduced FEV1 and FVC with an FEV1/FVC ratio of 0.89.
oneliner: 58F + 2 y exertional dyspnea + dry cough + bibasilar crackles + clubbing + FEV1/FVC 0.89 → lung volumes?
ask: Which set of lung volumes is most likely?

options.A: Functional residual capacity ↔, residual volume ↔, vital capacity ↔
options.B: Functional residual capacity ↑, residual volume ↑, vital capacity ↓
options.C: Functional residual capacity ↓, residual volume ↓, vital capacity ↑
options.D: Functional residual capacity ↔, residual volume ↑, vital capacity ↓
options.E: Functional residual capacity ↓, residual volume ↓, vital capacity ↓

whyNot.A: Her **FEV1 and FVC are reduced**, so volumes are not normal
whyNot.B: This is the **air-trapped** obstructive pattern; her **ratio of 0.89** is not low
whyNot.C: A **reduced FVC** means vital capacity is down, not up
whyNot.D: Raised residual volume implies **air trapping**, which a ratio of 0.89 argues against

answer: All volumes decreased: FRC ↓, RV ↓, VC ↓
why: Scarred, stiff lungs recoil inward harder, so the **balance with the chest wall settles at a lower FRC**, and every volume shrinks. The **FEV1/FVC ratio stays normal or high** because both fall together; a low ratio with air trapping is the obstructive pattern.
chain: Elastic recoil pulls the lungs smaller
FRC, RV and TLC all fall

idea.rule: Restrictive disease shrinks every volume; obstructive disease traps air and raises RV and FRC.
also: Sarcoidosis and asbestosis (other interstitial disease)
Drug-induced fibrosis (bleomycin, amiodarone)
Silicosis and other pneumoconioses
Chronic fibrotic hypersensitivity pneumonitis

stem: A sample of healthy adult whole blood, equilibrated with 16% O2, 5% CO2 and 79% N2 at 37 °C, has a P50 of about 26 mm Hg. Several manipulations are tried on separate aliquots.
oneliner: Adult whole blood, P50 26 mm Hg (16% O2, 5% CO2, 37 °C) → which manipulation raises P50?
ask: Which manipulation will increase the P50?

options.A: Equilibrating with gas containing 12% CO2 in place of 5%
options.D: Raising pH by 0.3 units with NaOH

whyNot.B: Cold **raises** oxygen affinity (left shift), so P50 falls
whyNot.C: Without 2,3-BPG, hemoglobin binds O2 **more tightly**, lowering P50
whyNot.D: Higher pH (Bohr effect) **raises affinity**, so P50 falls
whyNot.E: Fetal hemoglobin binds 2,3-BPG poorly and has **higher affinity**, lowering the mixed P50

why: More CO2 makes more H+ (lower pH), so the **Bohr effect** shifts the curve **right**: affinity falls and P50 rises. Heat, **2,3-BPG** and acid all do the same; cold, alkalosis, low 2,3-BPG and HbF do the opposite.
chain: Bohr effect: hemoglobin releases O2 more easily

idea.rule: Right shift (high P50) comes from more CO2, H+, temperature or 2,3-BPG; left shift is the opposite.
also: Exercising muscle (heat, acid, CO2)
Chronic altitude (more 2,3-BPG)
Anemia (more 2,3-BPG)
Fever

note: Source key was missing; answer follows the Bohr effect (12% CO2 lowers pH and right-shifts the curve).

stem: In a research laboratory, an oxygen-hemoglobin dissociation curve is plotted for a healthy volunteer's blood sample. The curve lies to the left of the standard curve, with a P50 below 26 mm Hg. Other conditions are controlled at standard values.
oneliner: Experiment: a blood sample's O2-Hb curve lies left of normal (P50 below 26) → what is different?
ask: Which change in the blood sample would best account for the shift?

options.C: A larger proportion of fetal hemoglobin

whyNot.A: 2,3-BPG binds the beta chains and **lowers affinity**, shifting the curve **right**
whyNot.B: Heat **lowers affinity** and shifts the curve **right**
whyNot.E: Acid shifts the curve **right**, again by the Bohr effect

why: A **left shift** means higher oxygen affinity and a **lower P50**. **Fetal hemoglobin** (alpha2 gamma2) binds 2,3-BPG poorly, so it holds oxygen more tightly. Increased 2,3-BPG, heat, CO2 and acid all **reduce** affinity and shift the curve right.
chain: Oxygen is harder to release but easier to take up from the placenta

idea.rule: Left shift = fewer right-shift factors: more HbF, CO, less BPG, cold, alkalosis.
also: Carbon monoxide and methemoglobin shift the curve left
Alkalosis and hypothermia shift it left
Stored blood loses 2,3-BPG and shifts left
Myoglobin binds oxygen even more tightly, with a far-left curve

stem: A 28-year-old man is found unresponsive after an opioid overdose, breathing 4 times a minute. He is intubated and placed on a ventilator that delivers a set volume at 12 breaths/min with 10 cm H2O of positive end-expiratory pressure (PEEP). Pressures are measured relative to the atmosphere.
oneliner: 28M + opioid overdose + RR 4, intubated, volume ventilation with PEEP 10 → alveolar and pleural pressures?
ask: Which set of pressures best describes the effect of ventilation on alveolar (PA) and intrapleural (Pip) pressure?

options.A: Peak inspiration: PA positive, Pip negative; end-expiration: PA zero, Pip negative
options.B: Peak inspiration: PA positive, Pip positive; end-expiration: PA positive, Pip positive
options.C: Peak inspiration: PA positive, Pip positive; end-expiration: both zero
options.D: Peak inspiration: PA negative, Pip negative; end-expiration: PA positive, Pip zero
options.E: Peak inspiration: PA zero, Pip negative; end-expiration: PA positive, Pip positive

whyNot.A: This is the **spontaneous-breathing** pattern, where the chest wall expands and Pip falls; a ventilator **pushes** gas in, so Pip rises
whyNot.C: This is ventilation **without PEEP**; he has **10 cm H2O of PEEP**, so pressures stay above zero at end-expiration
whyNot.D: Negative alveolar pressure at peak inspiration means gas is being **sucked** in; here the machine **pushes** it in
whyNot.E: A **positive-pressure** breath makes PA positive at peak inspiration, not zero, and Pip does not fall below zero

answer: Both pressures positive at peak inspiration and still positive at end-expiration
why: The ventilator **pushes** gas in, so alveolar pressure is positive and the expanding lung compresses the pleural space: **Pip becomes positive** at peak inspiration. **PEEP** holds the airways and alveoli above atmospheric pressure, so both stay positive at end-expiration instead of falling to zero (alveolar) and about -5 cm H2O (pleural). Raised intrathoracic pressure also **reduces venous return**.
chain: Ventilator drives gas in under pressure
Alveolar pressure becomes positive during the breath
Expanding lung transmits pressure to the pleural space: Pip positive
PEEP keeps both positive at end-expiration
Higher intrathoracic pressure lowers venous return

idea.rule: Positive-pressure ventilation reverses the normal pressure swing: Pip rises with each breath, and PEEP keeps alveolar and pleural pressure above baseline between breaths.
also: Spontaneous inspiration: PA dips slightly below zero and Pip falls to about -8 cm H2O
High PEEP in ARDS lowers preload and can drop cardiac output
Tension pneumothorax: Pip positive and venous return falls
Valsalva strain: intrathoracic pressure up, venous return down

stem: A 31-year-old man with pneumonia is sedated and mechanically ventilated. Each breath delivers 360 mL. Airway pressure at end-expiration is +6 cm H2O and at end-inspiration with flow stopped is +24 cm H2O. An esophageal balloon reads a pleural pressure of +12 cm H2O at end-inspiration.
oneliner: 31M + pneumonia, ventilated, VT 360 mL, airway pressure 6 → 24, pleural +12 → respiratory system compliance?
ask: What is this patient's respiratory system compliance?

whyNot.A: That is 360 divided by **24**, the end-inspiratory pressure alone; the **PEEP of 6** must be subtracted first
whyNot.B: That is 360 divided by **6**, the PEEP; compliance uses the **change** in airway pressure (6 to 24)
whyNot.C: That is the **inverse** (18 / 360), which is elastance in cm H2O per mL, not compliance
whyNot.E: That is 360 divided by 24 - **12**, using the **pleural pressure**; the ask is the whole respiratory system, so use airway pressure minus **PEEP**

why: Compliance is the **change in volume per change in pressure**. For the whole respiratory system on a ventilator the pressure change is **end-inspiratory airway pressure minus PEEP**: 24 - 6 = 18 cm H2O, so 360 / 18 = **20 mL/cm H2O**, low for an adult because the inflamed lung is stiff. The pleural pressure of +12 is not used.
chain: Pneumonia and edema stiffen the lung
More pressure is needed for the same volume

idea.rule: Ventilator compliance = tidal volume / (plateau airway pressure - PEEP); pleural pressure is used only for lung (not whole-system) compliance.
also: Static compliance uses plateau pressure, measured with flow stopped
Lung compliance alone uses the change in transpulmonary pressure (airway minus pleural pressure)
ARDS, pulmonary fibrosis and edema all lower compliance
Emphysema raises compliance

stem: A 41-year-old woman is brought in 30 minutes after taking a large amount of her sleeping tablets. She is drowsy, breathing 6 times a minute and shallowly, and has mild cyanosis on room air. Chest examination is clear, and there was no vomiting or aspiration.
oneliner: 41F + sleeping-pill overdose + RR 6, shallow, cyanosis on room air, clear lungs, no aspiration → ABG?
ask: Which set of arterial blood gas values (mm Hg) is most likely?

whyNot.B: Low PaCO2 means **hyperventilation**; she is breathing **6 times a minute**, so CO2 should rise
whyNot.C: PaCO2 fits, but a gradient of **30** says the lung also fails to transfer O2; her **chest is clear** with no aspiration
whyNot.D: She is **cyanotic on room air** and slow-breathing, so a normal PaO2 and PaCO2 do not fit
whyNot.E: Normal PaCO2 with a gradient of **50** is a shunt or diffusion defect; her lungs are **clear** and she hypoventilates

answer: PaO2 low, PaCO2 high, A-a gradient normal
why: A sedative depresses the respiratory centre, so **alveolar ventilation falls**: CO2 builds up and the alveolar PO2 falls with it (PAO2 = 150 - PaCO2/0.8 = about 62). Because the lung itself transfers gas normally, PaO2 falls to match and the **A-a gradient stays normal**.
chain: Alveolar PO2 falls as CO2 displaces O2
Lung exchange is normal, so the A-a gradient stays normal

idea.rule: Pure hypoventilation gives hypoxemia plus hypercapnia with a normal A-a gradient; a raised gradient means the lung is also diseased.
also: Opioid overdose
Obesity hypoventilation and neuromuscular weakness (Guillain-Barre, myasthenia)
High-altitude hypoxemia is also normal-gradient but with low PaCO2
Supplemental O2 corrects the hypoxemia of hypoventilation, but not the CO2

stem: A healthy 72-year-old woman has had pulmonary function tests and arterial blood gases every 5 years since age 22 as part of a research cohort. She never smoked and has no lung disease, but now has mild kyphosis and a stiffer rib cage.
oneliner: 72F + healthy lifelong never-smoker, serial PFTs and ABGs since age 22, kyphosis → changes now vs at 22?
ask: Which set of changes best describes her results now compared with age 22?

whyNot.A: Residual volume **rises** with age because small airways close earlier, trapping more gas
whyNot.B: The same lung changes impair matching, so **PaO2 falls** and the gradient widens even in health
whyNot.D: PaO2 does not rise with age; **earlier airway closure** worsens V/Q matching and lowers it
whyNot.E: Lost elastic recoil traps gas, so residual volume **goes up**, and PaO2 falls with the wider gradient

answer: Residual volume up, PaO2 down, A-a gradient up
why: With age the lung loses **elastic recoil** (compliance rises), so small airways close earlier and **residual volume increases**; the chest wall stiffens, and total lung capacity stays about the same. Dependent airway closure worsens V/Q matching, so **PaO2 falls and the A-a gradient widens**.
chain: Elastic fibres of the lung degrade
Small airways close earlier: RV rises
Stiff chest wall holds TLC about constant
More V/Q mismatch: PaO2 falls, A-a gradient rises

idea.rule: Aging: less lung recoil (compliance up), stiffer chest wall (compliance down), RV up, FVC and FEV1 down, TLC about unchanged, PaO2 down, A-a gradient up.
also: Emphysema shares the lost recoil and raised RV, but much more severely
Vital capacity falls as RV rises
PaCO2 stays normal in healthy aging
Closing volume rises with age and can exceed FRC when supine

stem: In a physiology laboratory, a volunteer breathes mixtures with rising CO2 and minute ventilation is plotted against arterial PCO2, giving a straight line that rises with PCO2. The measurement is repeated after the volunteer has been deeply anesthetized with an inhaled volatile agent (1.8 MAC).
oneliner: Experiment: ventilation vs PaCO2 line, repeated under deep volatile anesthesia → how does the line change?
ask: How does the ventilation-PaCO2 line change under deep anesthesia?

options.A: Shifts to the left and becomes steeper
options.B: Shifts to the left with the same slope
options.C: Same intercept with a steeper slope
options.D: No change in position or slope
options.E: Shifts to the right and becomes flatter

whyNot.A: A left, steeper line means **more** CO2 sensitivity (as with metabolic acidosis); anesthesia **depresses** the response
whyNot.B: A left shift is a **greater** response at any PCO2; anesthetics reduce it
whyNot.C: A steeper slope means a **stronger** response per mm Hg; deep anesthesia makes the response **weaker**
whyNot.D: Central chemoreceptors are **depressed** by volatile agents, so the response does change

answer: Right shift with a lower slope
why: Volatile anesthetics (like opioids and barbiturates) **depress the central chemoreceptor response**, so a higher PaCO2 is needed before ventilation starts and each rise in PaCO2 adds **less ventilation**: the line moves **right and flattens**. Metabolic acidosis does the opposite, a left shift.
chain: Brain responds less to a given PaCO2
More CO2 needed to start ventilation: curve shifts right
Each rise in PaCO2 adds less ventilation: slope falls

idea.rule: CNS depressants shift the CO2 response curve right and flatten it; metabolic acidosis or stimulants shift it left.
also: Opioid and barbiturate overdose
Sleep lowers the response slightly
Metabolic acidosis shifts the curve left (Kussmaul breathing)
Chronic CO2 retention blunts the central response, leaving hypoxic drive

stem: A 38-year-old woman falls from her bicycle and has severe pain over the right lower chest that is sharp and worsens when she coughs or inhales deeply. A chest radiograph shows fractures of three adjacent ribs. There is no pneumothorax and no lung contusion, and breath sounds are clear without wheezing.
oneliner: 38F + bicycle fall + 3 rib fractures, pain on deep breath or cough, no pneumothorax, no wheeze → respiratory change?
ask: Which set of changes in respiratory status is most likely?

options.A: Respiratory rate ↑, tidal volume ↓, airway resistance ↔
options.B: Respiratory rate ↑, tidal volume ↑, airway resistance ↔
options.C: Respiratory rate ↑, tidal volume ↓, airway resistance ↑
options.D: Respiratory rate ↓, tidal volume ↑, airway resistance ↔
options.E: Respiratory rate ↓, tidal volume ↓, airway resistance ↓

whyNot.B: Pain on deep breaths **limits** the volume she can take in, so tidal volume falls
whyNot.C: Her airways are **not narrowed** (**no wheeze**, no contusion, no pneumothorax), so resistance is unchanged
whyNot.D: She guards against **painful** deep breaths; slow, deep breathing would hurt more
whyNot.E: Pain makes her breathe **faster and shallower**, and nothing in the stem dilates her airways

answer: Faster, shallower breathing with unchanged airway resistance
why: Each deep breath moves the broken ribs, so she **splints**: she keeps each breath small (**tidal volume falls**) and breathes faster (**respiratory rate rises**) to hold minute ventilation. The airways themselves are not narrowed, so **resistance is unchanged**; the problem is the chest wall, not the lung.
chain: Rib fractures hurt on chest expansion
She avoids deep breaths: tidal volume falls
Minute ventilation maintained by a faster rate

idea.rule: Pain-limited breathing (splinting) lowers tidal volume and raises rate without changing airway resistance.
also: Pleurisy and pleuritic pain
Post-thoracotomy or upper abdominal surgery pain
Flail chest adds paradoxical motion
Restrictive disease gives the same rapid shallow pattern, with raised elastic work

stem: In an anesthetized, ventilated sheep, a catheter is placed in the main lymph duct draining the lungs, and lymph is collected over timed periods. Each of the following is given separately, and the animal is allowed to recover to baseline between trials.
oneliner: Sheep experiment: main pulmonary lymph duct cannulated, interventions given one at a time → which raises lymph flow?
ask: Which intervention will most likely increase pulmonary lymph flow?

options.B: Intravenous furosemide given as a single bolus
options.D: Phenylephrine injected into the pulmonary artery
options.E: Withdrawal of 15% of the blood volume

whyNot.A: Albumin **raises plasma oncotic pressure**, pulling fluid into the capillary and reducing filtration
whyNot.B: Furosemide **lowers plasma volume** (and dilates veins), so capillary hydrostatic pressure and filtration fall
whyNot.D: Phenylephrine constricts **upstream arterial** vessels as well, lowering downstream capillary pressure
whyNot.E: Blood loss **lowers vascular volume** and capillary hydrostatic pressure, so less fluid filters into the interstitium

why: Lymph carries away the fluid filtered by the **Starling forces**, so flow rises when filtration rises. A saline load **raises capillary hydrostatic pressure** and, by dilution, **lowers plasma oncotic pressure**, so net filtration and lymph flow increase. Albumin raises oncotic pressure, volume loss lowers capillary pressure, and upstream arterial constriction protects the capillaries.
chain: Plasma proteins are diluted: oncotic pressure falls
Net filtration into the interstitium increases

idea.rule: Lymph flow follows net capillary filtration: more hydrostatic pressure, less oncotic pressure or more permeability means more lymph.
also: Left heart failure raises pulmonary capillary pressure and lymph flow
Hypoalbuminemia lowers oncotic pressure
Increased capillary permeability (ARDS, histamine)
Lymph flow is the main safety factor against pulmonary edema

stem: A healthy 26-year-old woman moves from sea level to a town at 9,500 feet for a new job. Five weeks later she feels well and has no lung disease. Her respirations are slightly faster than before the move.
oneliner: 26F + healthy, sea level → 9,500 ft, now 5 weeks later, breathing slightly faster → ABG, bicarbonate, red cell mass?
ask: Which set of changes compared with her sea-level values is most likely?

options.A: PaO2 ↓, PaCO2 ↑, serum HCO3- ↑, red cell mass ↑
options.B: PaO2 ↓, PaCO2 ↓, serum HCO3- ↓, red cell mass ↑
options.C: PaO2 ↓, PaCO2 ↓, serum HCO3- ↑, red cell mass ↔
options.D: PaO2 ↔, PaCO2 ↓, serum HCO3- ↓, red cell mass ↑
options.E: PaO2 ↓, PaCO2 ↓, serum HCO3- ↔, red cell mass ↓

whyNot.A: Her breathing is **faster**, which lowers PaCO2; CO2 retention with raised bicarbonate fits chronic hypoventilation instead
whyNot.C: The kidney **excretes bicarbonate** to correct the alkalosis, so HCO3- falls; renal EPO also raises red cell mass
whyNot.D: Inspired PO2 is **lower** at 9,500 feet, so PaO2 falls even with faster breathing
whyNot.E: Chronic hypoxia drives **erythropoietin**, so red cell mass rises; and renal compensation lowers HCO3-

answer: Low PaO2, low PaCO2, low bicarbonate, more red cells
why: Low inspired PO2 lowers **PaO2**, and carotid-body drive increases ventilation, which lowers **PaCO2** and causes alkalosis. Over days the kidneys **excrete bicarbonate**, bringing pH back toward normal, while renal hypoxia raises **erythropoietin** and red cell mass over weeks.
chain: Barometric pressure falls: inspired and arterial PO2 fall
Carotid bodies increase ventilation: PaCO2 falls, pH rises
Kidneys excrete HCO3-, pH returns toward normal

idea.rule: Chronic altitude: PaO2 down, ventilation up (PaCO2 down), renal bicarbonate loss, EPO up (polycythemia).
also: Acetazolamide speeds acclimatization by wasting bicarbonate
Pulmonary vasoconstriction raises pulmonary artery pressure
2,3-BPG rises, shifting the O2-hemoglobin curve right
Acute mountain sickness occurs before acclimatization is complete

stem: A healthy 45-year-old man is on a long flight. The cabin is pressurised to a barometric pressure of 590 mm Hg. He breathes room air (21% oxygen), and inspired gas is fully humidified at 37 °C in the airways.
oneliner: 45M + airline cabin 590 mm Hg, room air, humidified at 37 °C → inspired PO2?
ask: What is his inspired PO2 (mm Hg), after humidification?

whyNot.A: That is 0.21 x 590 and **omits water vapor**; the humidified airway subtracts 47 mm Hg first
whyNot.B: That is the **sea-level** value near 0.21 x 713; cabin pressure here is lower
whyNot.C: That is an **alveolar** value (after subtracting PaCO2/R); inspired PO2 does not include CO2
whyNot.D: That subtracts the 47 mm Hg water vapor **after** multiplying by 0.21; it must be subtracted from the barometric pressure first

why: Inspired PO2 = FiO2 x (barometric pressure - water vapor pressure) = 0.21 x (590 - 47) = **114 mm Hg**. The **fraction of oxygen stays 0.21** at lower pressure; it is the total pressure that is lower, so the PO2 falls.

idea.rule: PIO2 = FiO2 x (PB - 47); altitude lowers PB but not FiO2.
also: Sea level: 0.21 x 713 = about 150 mm Hg
Alveolar PAO2 = PIO2 - PaCO2/R
Supplemental O2 raises FiO2 and so raises PIO2
Hypoxia at altitude comes from low PIO2, not from a lower O2 fraction

stem: A male newborn delivered at 29 weeks' gestation begins grunting and has chest retractions within an hour of birth. Amniotic fluid obtained earlier had a lecithin-to-sphingomyelin ratio of 1.4:1.
oneliner: Newborn boy, 29 weeks + grunting and retractions within 1 hour + L/S ratio 1.4:1 → lung mechanics?
ask: Which set of changes in the lungs is most likely?

whyNot.A: That is the **emphysema** pattern (lost recoil); this infant has a surfactant problem that raises surface tension
whyNot.B: Recoil and compliance move in **opposite** directions: stiffer lungs recoil harder, so compliance falls
whyNot.C: Recoil **rises** when surface tension is high; low recoil would mean easier, not harder, inflation
whyNot.E: Alveoli **collapse** at end-expiration, so FRC falls rather than rises

answer: Recoil up, compliance down, FRC down
why: An L/S ratio under 2 means **surfactant deficiency**, so alveolar **surface tension rises**. The lungs recoil harder and are stiffer (**compliance falls**), and alveoli collapse at end-expiration, so **FRC falls** and gas exchange suffers.
chain: Immature type II pneumocytes make too little surfactant
Alveoli collapse at end-expiration: FRC falls

idea.rule: Less surfactant means higher surface tension, so higher recoil, lower compliance, lower FRC (law of Laplace: smaller alveoli collapse).
also: ARDS also loses surfactant function, with stiff lungs and low FRC
Maternal diabetes delays surfactant maturation (fetal insulin inhibits it)
Pulmonary fibrosis moves the same way (recoil up, compliance down, FRC down) and also lowers TLC
Emphysema is the reverse: recoil down, compliance up, FRC up

stem: A 57-year-old woman is chatting over lunch when a crumb touches the back of her larynx and she coughs forcefully. The state of her glottis is considered at three moments: while she swallows, immediately after the laryngeal irritation, and during the explosive expulsion.
oneliner: 57F + chatting over lunch, crumb irritates larynx, coughs → glottis during swallow, just after irritation, during cough?
ask: Which sequence describes the glottis at those three moments?

whyNot.B: The glottis stays **closed** just after irritation so that pressure can build, and it must be **open**, not closed, for the expulsion
whyNot.C: The glottis is **closed during swallowing** to keep food out of the airway
whyNot.D: The glottis is **closed**, not open, in the compression phase just after irritation, while pressure builds
whyNot.E: It is **closed while swallowing**, not open, and it opens (not closes) for the cough itself

answer: Closed during swallowing, closed after irritation, open during the cough
why: During swallowing the glottis **closes** to protect the airway. After a laryngeal irritant, a deep inspiration is followed by **glottic closure** while the expiratory muscles contract, so intrathoracic pressure rises (compression phase). The glottis then **opens** suddenly and the pressure drives the explosive expulsion.
chain: Irritant triggers a reflex deep breath
Expiratory muscles contract: intrathoracic pressure rises
Glottis opens: explosive expiratory flow clears the irritant

idea.rule: Cough sequence: inspiration, glottis closes while expiratory muscles contract (pressure builds), glottis opens for the burst.
also: Valsalva also uses a closed glottis against expiratory effort
Sneeze: similar but expelled through the nose
Impaired glottic closure (vocal cord paralysis) gives a weak cough
